items.prompt: What does expected value multiply together for each outcome?
choices: Its cost and its duration
Its risk level and its effort
Its probability and its value
items.explanation: Each outcome contributes probability x value, and the contributions are added.

items.prompt: A coin pays $10 on heads and $0 on tails. What is the expected value of one flip?
A bike has a 5% chance of a $300 theft. What is the average loss?
All the outcome probabilities of one decision must add up to what?
choices: The largest payoff
Zero
items.explanation: The outcomes cover every case, so their probabilities total 1.

items.prompt: What sign does a cost get when you compute expected value?
choices: Negative
Positive
It is left out
items.explanation: A loss counts against you, so its value is negative.

items.prompt: A 10% chance of $100 and a 90% chance of $0. What is the expected value?
In the unit, what is the expected value of migrating now?
Why does waiting win in the unit's numbers?
choices: Its expected value is higher: +$3,900 against −$700
Its payoff when things go well is much larger than the other option's
It carries no outage risk, so its average cannot be dragged below zero
items.explanation: Waiting has both a lower outage chance and a still-positive payoff, so its average is higher.

items.prompt: Option A: a 10% chance of losing $1,000, otherwise nothing. Option B: a 50% chance of losing $150, otherwise nothing. Which costs less on average?
choices: A, whose loss is far less likely than B's, at 10% against 50%
B, whose average loss is $75 against $100 for A
They tie, because both options can end with no loss at all
A, whose worst case is a $1,000 loss rather than B's $150
items.explanation: A averages 0.10 x 1,000 = $100 of loss; B averages 0.50 x 150 = $75. The rarer risk is not the cheaper one when its loss is much bigger.
items.reference:
Weigh each outcome by its odds
EV = sum of (probability x value)
no lock: 0.05 x 300 = $15 average loss
padlock: $8 + 0.01 x 300 = $11
migrate now: −$700 | wait: +$3,900
Why: a chance and an amount only mean something together, so multiply them and add.
items.learnMore:
Weigh each outcome by its odds

Expected value turns a risky choice into one comparable number by weighting every possible outcome by how often it happens. Costs are negative values, and the probabilities of one decision must add to 1.

Common mistake

Comparing only the probabilities (2% is safer than 15%) and forgetting the payoffs that sit behind them.
items.reflection: Think of a decision you made by gut feeling. What were its possible outcomes, and what rough odds and amounts would you put on each?

Nothing is wrong, since an EV can be computed from any two branches

items.prompt: A server has a 4% chance of a $20,000 incident this year. A $500 mitigation cuts the chance to 1%. Is it worth it on average?
choices: Yes: it removes a $20,000 risk for a mere $500
No: the 1% left over is still a risk of $20,000
No: the $500 is a sure cost against a loss that may never come
Yes: expected cost falls from $800 to $700 ($500 plus $200)
items.explanation: Without it: 0.04 x 20,000 = 800. With it: 500 + 0.01 x 20,000 = 700. It saves $100 on average under these assumed figures; a sure cost is compared with an average, not with "may never come".

items.prompt: EV(migrate now) is −$700. What does one migration actually end at?
choices: Exactly −$700
Somewhere between the two outcomes
items.explanation: A single attempt lands on one listed outcome; −700 is never one of them.

items.prompt: What does an expected value describe?
choices: The most likely single result
The long-run average over many repeats
The best result that can happen on a lucky day
items.explanation: It averages every outcome weighted by its probability.

items.prompt: A game pays $10 or $0 and has an EV of $5. Can one play end with exactly $5?
choices: Yes, always
Only on the second play of the game
No: it ends at $10 or $0
items.explanation: The EV is an average, not one of the listed payouts.

items.prompt: Which team gets closest to its EV?
choices: One that repeats many similar decisions
One that decides once
One that avoids all risky decisions altogether
items.explanation: More repeats let the average settle toward the EV.

items.prompt: Does a positive EV guarantee a profit on a single attempt?
choices: Yes
No
Only if the win chance is above 50%
items.explanation: A single attempt can still hit a losing branch.

items.prompt: You repeat a bet many times. The average result moves toward what?
choices: The best single outcome
The worst single outcome
The expected value
items.explanation: That is what the long-run average means.

items.prompt: A migration with EV −$700 happens to end at +$8,000. Was the EV calculation wrong?
choices: No: one outcome can differ from the average
Yes: the probabilities must have been wrong
Yes: EV must equal the result
items.explanation: The average describes many attempts, not this one.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses EV correctly?
choices: This bet will lose exactly $700 today
Over many bets like this we lose about $700 on average
This bet cannot win under any outcome
items.explanation: EV talks about the average of many repeats.

items.prompt: A team takes three bets that each have a positive EV and loses money on all three. What can you conclude?
choices: The EV was wrong, because a positive EV rules out three losses in a row
Nothing about the EV: three draws are too few to reveal an average
The probabilities must be wrong, since losing three times is impossible
The team should stop, since a loss streak overrides any EV
items.explanation: A positive EV is compatible with losing several times in a row; only a long run shows the average. Three losses can be a bad streak, not proof of bad inputs.
items.reference:
Average over repeats, not a forecast
single attempt: lands on +$8,000 or −$50,000
−$700 is the long-run average of many bets
many similar decisions: the average shows up
one decision: only one draw
Why: the expected value is a property of the whole set of outcomes, not of any one result.

EV applies only to gains and never to a loss
items.explanation: The −$700 is a probability-weighted mix of two outcomes; the single attempt ends at one of them. It is also the less likely branch that costs $50,000 (15%).

items.prompt: In a decision tree, what does a square node represent?
choices: A choice you control
A chance outcome
A final payoff written at the end of a branch
items.explanation: Squares are decisions; circles are chance.

items.prompt: What does a circle (chance) node represent?
choices: A choice that you make yourself
Something that happens by chance
A cost that is added at the end
items.explanation: The branches out of it are outcomes with probabilities.

items.prompt: The probabilities leaving one chance node must sum to what?
items.explanation: The branches must cover every outcome exactly once.

items.prompt: In which direction do you evaluate a decision tree?
choices: From the leaves back toward the root
From the root forward, one level at a time
From the middle outward in both directions
items.explanation: Later values feed the nodes before them.

items.prompt: Where does a third option go on the tree?
choices: It needs a whole new tree of its own
As another branch off the same decision node
It replaces the first option that was drawn
items.explanation: Any number of options can leave one decision node.

items.prompt: What does a decision node pick?
choices: The branch with the highest probability
The branch with the lowest payoff
The branch with the highest EV
items.explanation: It compares the EVs of its options and takes the best.

items.prompt: A chance node has branches of 15% and 80%. Is it valid?
choices: No: they add to 95%
Yes
Yes, if the payoffs are equal
items.explanation: A missing 5% means the weighted sum is not an average.

items.prompt: In the unit, what is the EV of the "wait" chance node?
A chance node is drawn with three branches at 30% each. What is wrong with it?
choices: Three branches are too many for a single chance node
The probabilities add to 90%, leaving 10% unaccounted for
The branches should add to 100 rather than to 1
Nothing is wrong, since equal branches always balance
items.explanation: The branches must cover every outcome exactly, so they add to 1 (100%). Here 10% is missing, so any weighted sum is not a true average.
items.reference:
Draw it as a tree, solve from the leaves
square: a choice you control
circle: chance you do not control
probabilities out of a chance node add to 1
solve right to left: chance nodes become EVs, decision nodes take the max
Why: a tree separates what you choose from what happens to you, so every probability and payoff has one place.
items.learnMore:
Draw it as a tree, solve from the leaves

Evaluate from the leaves back: each chance node becomes the sum of probability x value of its branches, each decision node takes its best option. Adding another option is just another branch off the same decision node.

Common mistake

Letting the probabilities leaving a chance node fall short of, or exceed, 1.

items.prompt: What is a break-even probability?
choices: The chance at which an outage becomes completely certain
The chance at which two options have equal EV
The smallest chance that exists
items.explanation: Below or above it, the better option changes.

items.prompt: In the unit, migrating now beats waiting only when the outage chance is below about what?
Why compute a break-even point?
choices: To see how wrong an estimate can be before the choice flips
To make the guessed estimate become an exact figure
To remove the need for any probabilities at all
items.explanation: It tests how robust the decision is to a guessed input.

items.prompt: If the real outage chance for migrating now were 5%, which option would have the higher EV?
choices: Waiting, at its fixed EV of $3,900
Migrating now (about $5,100)
A tie at that chance

items.prompt: If a failed migration would cost more than $50,000, the break-even outage chance moves which way?
choices: Higher
It does not change
Lower
items.explanation: A bigger loss makes each point of risk more expensive, so it takes a smaller chance to tie.

items.prompt: The assumed 15% is far above the 7% break-even. The decision is therefore what?
choices: Fairly robust: waiting wins unless the guess is badly off
Impossible to decide until the odds are known exactly
Certain to be right whatever the true odds turn out to be
items.explanation: The guess would have to be wrong by more than half before the choice flips.

items.prompt: An estimate sits right next to the break-even. What does that mean?
choices: The decision is easy and can be made at once
The decision is sensitive to it and deserves more work
The estimate must be exactly right to be used
items.explanation: Small errors would flip the choice.

items.prompt: On the unit's chart, what does the line crossing zero mean?
choices: An outage has become certain at that point
Both options lose money at that point
The two options have equal EV
items.explanation: It plots the difference of the two EVs, so zero means a tie.

items.prompt: Nobody can rule out a 6% outage chance for migrating now (break-even about 7.07%). What follows?
choices: Robust, since 6% is close to the 7% break-even and so changes little
Not robust: at 6% migrating now is worth $4,520, above waiting's $3,900
Robust, because waiting is the safer option whatever the odds are
Nothing follows until the chance is known down to the decimal
items.explanation: 8,000 − 58,000 x 0.06 = 4,520 > 3,900, so a plausible estimate flips the answer. That is exactly the kind of fragility the break-even check is meant to expose.
items.reference:
Where the answer flips
migrate now: EV = 8000 − 58000p
wait: EV = 3,900 (fixed)
equal at p = 4100 / 58000, about 7.07%
at the assumed 15%, the gap is −$4,600
Why: the break-even shows how wrong an estimate can be before your choice changes.
items.learnMore:
Where the answer flips

Hold one option fixed, let the uncertain probability vary and find where the two EVs are equal. If your plausible range for the guess sits entirely on one side, the decision is robust; if it straddles the break-even, investigate that input.

Common mistake

Treating one guessed probability as exact and never asking what happens if it is off.
items.reflection: Which estimate behind a decision of yours is the shakiest? How far could it be off before you would choose differently?

Waiting rises too, because the payoffs are linked
items.explanation: 0.15 x (−50,000) + 0.85 x 14,000 = −7,500 + 11,900 = 4,400. The success payoff matters as well as the odds: the threshold is about $13,412.

items.prompt: When can a better expected value still be the wrong choice?
choices: When the probabilities of the outcomes add up to 1
When the same decision is repeated very often
When one outcome is a loss you cannot recover from
items.explanation: You need to survive to collect the long-run average.

items.prompt: What does a one-off decision get?
choices: A single draw, not the average
The average of many draws of the same bet
A guaranteed result
items.explanation: The average only appears across repeats.

items.prompt: Three tries each with a 15% outage chance. What is the chance of at least one outage?
choices: About 39%
45% exactly

items.prompt: A startup with $55,000 faces a possible $50,000 loss. That loss is what?
choices: Irrelevant to the decision
Certainly acceptable
Potentially unrecoverable
items.explanation: It would leave almost nothing to carry on with.

items.prompt: For a decision repeated often with survivable losses, what is a sound default?
choices: Follow the higher expected value
Choose by gut feeling
Always take the lowest-risk option
items.explanation: Over many repeats the averages win out.

items.prompt: The survival correction is applied how?
choices: Instead of EV
On top of EV, not instead of it
Only after the decision is made
items.explanation: Compute EV first, then look at the size and chance of any ruinous branch.

items.prompt: Two options share the same ruinous loss. What should you compare?
choices: Only which option has more outcomes drawn
Only which option is cheaper to start with
How likely that loss is under each
items.explanation: The same size of loss is more dangerous when it happens more often.

items.prompt: Why does ruin break the logic of averaging?
choices: There is no next attempt to average over
The probabilities stop adding up to 1 after a large loss
Expected value is simply not defined for large losses
items.explanation: A loss that ends the game removes all later repeats.

items.prompt: A company with $55,000 in cash compares X (EV +$8,000, a 10% chance of a $60,000 loss) and Y (EV +$2,000, no chance of a loss above $5,000). Which is the better choice?
choices: X, because its expected value is four times as large as Y's
Y, since X has a 10% chance of a loss above its cash
X, because 90% of the time it avoids any loss at all
Y, because it has the smaller payoff to put at risk
items.explanation: X's average is better but one branch is unrecoverable and happens one time in ten. Y's worst case is survivable. (All figures are illustrative assumptions.)
items.reference:
A good average, a risk you cannot survive
three tries at 15%: 1 − 0.85³ ≈ 38.6% of at least one outage
one-shot decision: one draw, no average
unrecoverable loss: no next attempt
survivable and repeated: follow the higher EV
Why: the long-run average only helps if you stay in the game long enough to collect it.
items.learnMore:
A good average, a risk you cannot survive

EV is the right first number, but it hides how a single loss could end things and how small repeated risks add up. When a branch is unrecoverable, compare the chance of that branch across options as well as the averages.

Common mistake

Following the higher EV into a loss the business cannot absorb.
items.reflection: What is the loss in your own life or work that you could not recover from? How often are you exposed to it?

items.prompt: A task has a 2% outage chance and is run 10 times independently. What is the chance of at least one outage?
choices: About 20%
About 2%
About 18%
About 12%
items.explanation: 1 − 0.98^10 is about 0.183. Adding 10 x 2% = 20% overcounts, because runs with two outages are counted twice.
items.reference:
A good average, a risk you cannot survive
three tries at 15%: 1 − 0.85³ ≈ 38.6% of at least one outage
one-shot decision: one draw, no average
unrecoverable loss: no next attempt
survivable and repeated: follow the higher EV
Why: the long-run average only helps if you stay in the game long enough to collect it.
items.learnMore:
A good average, a risk you cannot survive

EV is the right first number, but it hides how a single loss could end things and how small repeated risks add up. When a branch is unrecoverable, compare the chance of that branch across options as well as the averages.

Common mistake

Following the higher EV into a loss the business cannot absorb.
items.reflection: What is the loss in your own life or work that you could not recover from? How often are you exposed to it?

items.prompt: A large company makes a migration choice like this one every month, and its worst case is survivable. What is the sound guidance?
choices: Follow the higher EV, since many repeats let the average show
Avoid the higher EV, since any outage would be intolerable
Decide by the best case, since the losses are survivable anyway
Ignore EV, since every single decision is different from the last
items.explanation: Frequent decisions with survivable worst cases are where EV works best, because the average has room to appear.

items.prompt: Someone argues "the EV is positive, so the risk is fine." Which question is missing?
choices: Is the EV big enough to be rounded to a whole number?
Are there more than two outcomes drawn in the tree?
Is the positive EV mostly driven by the one largest payoff?
Could any branch be unrecoverable, and how likely is it?
items.explanation: EV does not show whether one branch would end the business. That check sits on top of the average.

items.prompt: Which node do you solve first in a two-stage tree?
choices: The first chance node, nearest the root
The root alone, before anything else
The last decision, nearest the leaves
items.explanation: Later values feed the earlier nodes.

items.prompt: The index bet pays +$2,000 (60%) or −$4,000 (40%). What is its EV?
Given the index bet's EV, should you switch it on?
choices: Yes: it can pay $2,000
No: its EV is negative
Yes: any bet is worth taking
items.explanation: You skip a bet whose average is below zero.

items.prompt: A decision node after a chance branch has what value?
choices: The average of its options
The value of its first option
The value of its best option
items.explanation: You choose the best option at a decision node.

items.prompt: Once a sub-tree is solved, how do you treat it?
choices: As one number in the node before it
As a separate tree that can be ignored
As one more probability on the branch
items.explanation: Its value replaces the whole sub-tree.

items.prompt: Why start from the leaves?
choices: Leaves are always the largest numbers in the tree
Later values set the value of the earlier branches
The root has no probabilities attached to it
items.explanation: Stage 1 needs to know what you would do afterwards.

items.prompt: Skipping the index, what is stage 1's EV in the unit?
A later bet has an EV of +$1,400. What should you do at that decision?
choices: Take it
Skip it
Wait for a bigger one
items.explanation: A positive EV beats the zero of skipping.

items.prompt: The index bet pays +$5,000 (60%) or −$4,000 (40%) on top of the $8,000. What is stage 1's EV once the later choice is folded back?
items.explanation: The bet's EV is +1,400, so you take it: the success branch is 9,400 and stage 1 is −7,500 + 0.85 x 9,400 = 490. +1,400 is only the bet; +700 just adds the bet's 1,400 to −700.
items.reference:
Solve the last decision first
index bet alone: 0.6 x 2,000 + 0.4 x (−4,000) = −$400
success branch: max(skip 8,000, switch on 7,600) = 8,000
stage 1: 0.15 x (−50,000) + 0.85 x 8,000 = −$700
payoff +5,000 instead: bet EV +$1,400, stage 1 EV $490
Why: a later choice sets the value of the branch before it, so it has to be solved first.
items.learnMore:
Solve the last decision first

Fold from the leaves: the value of a decision node is its best option, and that number then replaces the whole sub-tree in the chance node before it. Forcing a bad option instead of choosing the best one lowers the value of every branch above it.

Common mistake

Plugging a placeholder value into the earlier branch instead of solving the later decision first.
items.reflection: Think of a plan of yours with a second choice that only exists if the first thing works out. How would that later choice change what the first step is worth?

items.prompt: Why can stage 1 not be evaluated before the later skip-or-switch decision?
choices: The later decision has the larger probabilities on it
Chance nodes cannot be computed before decision nodes
The success branch is worth whichever later option is better
The later options are drawn to the right of the tree
items.explanation: Stage 1 is built from its branch values, and one branch's value is the best of its later options. Without solving it you are guessing that branch's value.

items.prompt: A team assumes it must switch the index on after a fine migration. What is stage 1's EV then, and what does it show?
choices: −$700: the later choice can never matter to stage 1
+$490: forcing a bet can only ever add value overall
−$1,040: which is the same as simply skipping the bet
−$1,040: forcing a bad option lowers every branch above it
items.explanation: The success branch becomes 7,600, so 0.15 x (−50,000) + 0.85 x 7,600 = −1,040, which is $340 below the −700 you get by choosing to skip.

items.prompt: What can a simulation of the bet confirm?
choices: That the inputs are true in the real world
That the decision is a wise one to make
That the arithmetic follows from the inputs
items.explanation: It replays the stated probabilities and payoffs.

items.prompt: What happens if the input probabilities are wrong?
choices: The EV is confidently wrong
The code throws an error and stops at once
The EV becomes zero
items.explanation: Garbage in, precise garbage out.

items.prompt: As the number of trials grows, the typical gap from the true EV does what?
choices: Grows
Shrinks
Stays fixed
items.explanation: It falls roughly with the square root of the trials.

items.prompt: Why run a simulation with several seeds?
choices: To make the answer exact
To choose the luckiest run and report that
To check that the results agree
items.explanation: A real bug fails every run; noise scatters.

items.prompt: Ten times the trials shrinks the typical gap by about what factor?
items.explanation: The gap falls with the square root of 10, about 3.16.

items.prompt: Where do the unit's 15% and $50,000 come from?
choices: A measured dataset from production systems
They are assumptions
A published study
items.explanation: They are stated as illustrative figures.

items.prompt: What does a break-even check test?
choices: Whether the code compiles without any errors
Whether the simulation ran for long enough
How wrong an input can be before the choice flips
items.explanation: It is a robustness test on an input.

items.prompt: A single small run lands far from the exact EV. What is the likely cause?
choices: Sampling noise
A broken formula
A wrong sign
items.explanation: Small samples scatter widely around the true value.

items.prompt: A 1,000-trial simulation of migrate now averages −$1,338 against an exact −$700; the typical gap at 1,000 trials is about $655. What is the most reasonable reading?
choices: A bug in the formula, since the result is $638 off
Ordinary sampling noise, about one typical gap away
Proof that 15% is too low an outage chance
A sign the simulation should be trusted over the formula
items.explanation: The difference is 638, close to one typical gap of 655. A real bug would persist across seeds; noise averages out.
items.reference:
A simulation checks the arithmetic, not the guess
simulation: checks the arithmetic follows from the inputs
typical gap = 20,710 / sqrt(trials)
1,000 trials: about $655; 100,000: about $65
break-even odds: tests how wrong an input can be
Why: a precise-looking EV is only as good as its guessed probabilities and payoffs.
items.learnMore:
A simulation checks the arithmetic, not the guess

Simulation shows that your formula and code agree, and the standard error shows how noisy a sample average is. Neither says whether 15% is the real outage chance; only sensitivity checks and better evidence address that.

Common mistake

Reading a close match between simulation and formula as proof that the inputs are right.
items.reflection: Which number in a plan you have seen looked precise but was really a guess? How could you test how much it matters?

items.prompt: The typical gap is proportional to one over the square root of the trials. How many times more trials halve it?
choices: 2 times
8 times
4 times
16 times
items.explanation: Halving needs the square root of the trials to double, so the trials must quadruple.

items.prompt: Which check best addresses doubt about the 15% outage estimate?

Rounding the EV to the nearest whole dollar again
Re-adding the probabilities to confirm they still total 1

items.prompt: Implement `expectedValue(outcomes)`: each outcome is `{ p, v }`. Return the sum of `p * v`. Assume the probabilities are valid.
items.explanation: Each outcome contributes its probability times its value, and the contributions are added.

items.prompt: Implement `expectedLoss(p, loss)`: the average loss of a risk with chance `p` of losing `loss`. Round the result to cents.
items.explanation: The average loss is the chance times the amount; rounding to cents hides floating-point noise.

items.prompt: Implement `isValidDistribution(ps)`: return true when the probabilities in the array add up to 1 (allow a tolerance of 1e-9).
items.explanation: Adding floats can leave tiny errors, so the total is compared with a tolerance instead of with ===.

items.prompt: Implement `bestLabel(options)`: each option is `{ label, ev }`. Return the label of the option with the highest `ev`.
items.explanation: A decision node takes the option with the highest expected value.

items.prompt: Implement `padlockSaving(lockCost, pBefore, pAfter, loss)`: the expected money saved by buying the lock, that is the drop in expected loss minus the lock cost. Round to cents.
items.explanation: The lock saves (pBefore − pAfter) x loss on average, and its cost comes off that. A negative result means it costs more than it saves.

items.prompt: Implement `evOfBet(p, win, lose)`: a bet wins `win` with chance `p`, otherwise loses `lose` (a positive number). Return its expected value rounded to cents.
items.explanation: The win counts with probability p, the loss with probability 1 − p, and the loss enters as a subtraction.

items.prompt: Implement `shouldTake(ev)`: return true when a bet is worth taking on expected value alone (strictly positive).
items.explanation: Skipping is worth zero, so a bet must be strictly better than zero to be worth taking.

items.prompt: Implement `sumProbabilities(ps)`: return the total of the probabilities, rounded to 4 decimal places.
items.explanation: Adding 0.1 and 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004, so rounding is needed before comparing or showing the total.

items.prompt: Implement `expectedValue(outcomes)`: each outcome is `{ p, v }`. Throw an `Error` if the probabilities do not add to 1 (tolerance 1e-9). Otherwise return the sum of `p * v` rounded to cents.

tests.expr: expect(() => expectedValue([{ p: 0.15, v: -50000 }, { p: 0.8, v: 8000 }])).toThrow()

items.explanation: The check runs before the result is trusted: a list that does not total 1 has no average. Rounding to cents removes floating-point noise.
items.reference:
Compute it, and refuse a broken distribution
expected value = sum of p x v
check the p values add to 1 before trusting the sum
round to cents to hide floating-point noise
a tree folds this at every chance node, max at every decision
Why: writing the calculation is where an unchecked probability list turns into a confident wrong number.
items.learnMore:
Compute it, and refuse a broken distribution

The core is one multiply-and-add. The part that needs care is validation (probabilities must total 1) and floating point: 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3, so compare with a tolerance and round results.

Common mistake

Returning a number from a probability list that does not add to 1.
items.reflection: Where else do you add up weighted pieces and never check that the weights make sense? What would the equivalent of the sum-to-1 check be?

items.prompt: Implement `breakEvenProbability(okValue, lossValue, rivalEv)`: a risky option gives `okValue` with chance 1 − p and `lossValue` with chance p. Return the p at which its EV equals `rivalEv`, rounded to 4 decimal places.
items.explanation: EV = okValue(1 − p) + lossValue p = okValue − p(okValue − lossValue). Setting it equal to rivalEv and solving gives p = (okValue − rivalEv) / (okValue − lossValue).

items.prompt: Implement `foldTree(node)`. A leaf is `{ value }`. A chance node is `{ chance: [{ p, node }, ...] }` and is worth the sum of `p * foldTree(node)`. A decision node is `{ choose: [node, ...] }` and is worth its best option. Round every result to cents.

tests.expr: expect(foldTree({ chance: [{ p: 0.02, node: { value: -50000 } }, { p: 0.98, node: { value: 5000 } }] })).toBe(3900)

expect(foldTree({ chance: [{ p: 0.15, node: { value: -50000 } }, { p: 0.85, node: { choose: [{ value: 8000 }, { chance: [{ p: 0.6, node: { value: 10000 } }, { p: 0.4, node: { value: 4000 } }] }] } }] })).toBe(-700)

expect(foldTree({ chance: [{ p: 0.15, node: { value: -50000 } }, { p: 0.85, node: { choose: [{ value: 8000 }, { chance: [{ p: 0.6, node: { value: 13000 } }, { p: 0.4, node: { value: 4000 } }] }] } }] })).toBe(490)

items.explanation: Leaves return their value. A chance node adds p times the solved sub-tree, a decision node takes the best solved option. Solving sub-trees first is exactly the fold-back from the leaves.
